newsitem.title: KENYA: 15 Kenyan policemen detained over student killings.
newsitem.headline: 15 Kenyan policemen detained over student killings.

text.p: Kenyan police have detained 15 of their colleagues following the killing of two students during a demonstration at Nairobi's Kenyatta University, a police spokesman said on Thursday.
The two students died on Wednesday when police opened fire during a protest against the police killing of a student at Egerton University in Njoro on Tuesday.

Senior Superintendent Peter Kimanthi at police headquarters in Nairobi said police firearms were taken for ballistic tests to identify who fired the fatal shots "so that we can charge them in court as soon as possible with the offence or offences."
"We are holding 15 of them," he said.
Kimanthi said a public inquest would be held into the death of the Egerton student whom he said had been shot when students tried to snatch guns from 20 policemen.
A government statement issued on Wednesday said action would be taken against those reponsible for these "unfortunate acts".
It said police were called in after a report that Kenyatta University students were on the rampage, stoning cars, building barricades and lighting fires on a main road outside the campus.
"Police shot in the air several times as a result of which the students ran back to the campus from where they engaged the police in a running battle," the government statement said.

"The police continued firing in the air as the skirmishes continued. The government is deeply saddened by the police action which led to the death of two students and serious injuries to three others," the statement added.

But George Eshiwani, Kenyatta University's vice-chancellor, said the student protests were peaceful and that he gave firm instructions police should not enter the campus on Wednesday because students were mourning their dead colleague.
"The students were not violent in any way. Why? Why had this to happen? You only needed to fire teargas and nothing more," he was quoted as telling a police officer after the shooting.
Police Commissioner Shedrach Kiruki told Nairobi newspapers police should have had only rubber bullets to disperse students.
The East African Standard newspaper quoted a policeman at Kenyatta University as saying police ran out of teargas to disperse students so had no alternative but to fire bullets.
The student movement in Kenya in the 1980s had a political agenda and at times challenged the ruling establishment.
But it has been reduced in recent years to sporadic protests over money and poor conditions at universities largely because of internal divisions based on tribal differences.

The Egerton University students were protesting over a refund of 504 shillings ($9.89) they said each of them was owed by the administration. The students also wanted the release of one of their leaders remanded by a court for inciting violence.
Kenyatta University closed on Wednesday for Christmas, instead of Friday, because of the killings.
